check_plant_status.description: Answer "may I plant this here, and must I remove it?" in one step. USDA keeps three separate lists - the noxious weeds a state regulates by law, the plants it publishes as invasive, and the species protected as threatened or endangered - and this reads all three and reports them together, with a one-sentence summary you can put straight into a message. Narrow it to a state to get the answer for that state alone. No API key required.

find_plants.description: Search the USDA PLANTS database by any part of a name. It matches common names, scientific names and PLANTS symbols at once, so "milkweed", "Asclepias" and "ASCLE" all find the milkweeds, and older scientific names find the plant they were renamed to. Every result comes back with its symbol, its botanical name without the naming authority, and a link to its page - so this is the step that turns what somebody typed into something the other steps can use. No API key required.

get_growing_conditions.description: Get what USDA records about how a plant grows: the soil textures and pH range it tolerates, how much drought, shade, salt and fire it takes, how fast it grows and how tall it gets, when it blooms and what colour, how it is propagated, and what it is used for. Up to 81 attributes, grouped the way USDA groups them, with the dozen a workflow usually branches on lifted to the top so drought tolerance is a field rather than a row to go hunting for. USDA has this detail for a minority of its plants; the record says when it has none. No API key required.

description: Look up any plant in the USDA PLANTS Database - the federal record of every plant in the United States and its territories. Search by common name, scientific name or symbol and get the accepted name, the family, whether it is native or introduced where you are, how it grows, what it tolerates and when it blooms. Check in one step whether a plant is a regulated noxious weed, listed as invasive, or protected as threatened or endangered, in any state or federally - or pull a state's whole weed list to check a catalogue against. Wetland indicator status, photographs and USDA's own fact sheets come back as links you can send. No account and no API key: it is public data from the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service.
